## Previously ...

The era before "reading the code of life" — discriminating DNA and proteins mainly by their **physical properties**: size and charge.

::: {.incremental}
- **Gel electrophoresis** — simple, rapid, sensitive;
- different ways to *create patterns*:
  - **restrictases** — site-specific cutting;
  - **PCR** — primer-specific amplification;
  - **combinations** of the two.
- These methods are **still relevant today**.
:::

## Molekulaarsete andmete eelised

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="62%"}
- DNA ja valgu järjestused on rangelt **pärilikud** (arvestada tuleb horisontaalse geeniülekande võimalusega ja sugulise paljunemise puhul homoloogse rekombinatsiooniga);
- tunnuste — nukleotiidi- või aminohappepositsioonide — ja tunnuse seisundite kirjeldus on **üheselt mõistetav**;
- tunnused on **sõltumatud**: asendus ühes positsioonis ei mõjuta asendumist teistes;
- andmed on **kvantitatiivselt kergemini töödeldavad**, saab kasutada matemaatilisi meetodeid;
- võimaldavad võrrelda **väga kaugeid organisme**;
- **informatsiooni suur hulk**: imetaja genoom ~3 miljardit nukleotiidipaari, bakteri genoom 0.5 – >10 miljonit.
:::

## Molecular genetic markers

::: {.incremental}
- Molecular markers can address ecological questions that are **difficult to pursue in any other way**.
- A primary advantage: markers and their variation can be **quantified with greater precision** than most other ecological measurements — better data for statistical comparison.
- They have become instrumental in understanding the patterns and processes behind **extant global biodiversity**.
- Using a marker means taking a **sample from the whole genome** — and any sample carries **sampling error**.
- A single marker type and a small number of loci **increases that error** and can lead to misinterpretation.
:::

## DNA and DNA — different sources

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
- **Eukaryotes**: genomic DNA (gDNA), chloroplast DNA (cpDNA), mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA);
- **Prokaryotes**: chromosomal DNA, plasmids, cloning vectors;
- **microbial community** — the metagenome;
- **ncDNA** — non-coding DNA;
- **eDNA** — environmental DNA;
- **aDNA** — ancient DNA;
- **cDNA** — complementary DNA synthesised from an mRNA template.
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
![](/assets/loeng4/p05_1.jpg)
:::
:::

## Genomics

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
Whole genome sequences are rapidly becoming available for a wide range of organisms. **Comparative genomics** uses megabases of data — rather than short sequences from a few genes — to build phylogenies and investigate the mechanisms of speciation.

- **Pan genome** — all genes and genetic variation within a species;
- **Core genome** — the portion common to all individuals;
- **Dispensable genome** — the portion present only in a subset, or unique to individuals.
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
![](/assets/loeng4/p06_1.jpg)
:::
:::

## Comparative genomics

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](/assets/loeng4/p07_1.jpg)
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](/assets/loeng4/p07_2.jpg)
:::
:::

A large-scale, holistic approach: compare two or more genomes to find similarities and differences, and study the biology of each — a highly detailed view of how organisms are related **at the gene level**.

## Non-nuclear DNA

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
::: {.incremental}
- **High copy number.** A mitochondrion or chloroplast holds multiple copies of its DNA, and a cell holds many organelles — often thousands of copies per cell.
- **Random segregation.** Organelles are randomly distributed to daughter cells during mitosis and meiosis.
- **Single-parent inheritance.** Non-nuclear DNA is often inherited uniparentally — in humans, mitochondrial DNA comes from the mother.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
![](/assets/loeng4/p08_1.jpg)
:::
:::

## Endosymbiosis

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](/assets/loeng4/p09_1.jpg)
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](/assets/loeng4/p09_2.jpg)
:::
:::

Similarities between the DNA of mitochondria and chloroplasts and the DNA of **bacteria** are an important line of evidence for the **endosymbiont theory** — that both originated as free-living prokaryotic cells.

## Vertical vs horizontal gene transfer

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
![](/assets/loeng4/p10_1.jpg){height="400px"}
:::
::: {.column width="55%"}
**Vertical** gene transfer happens between generations.

**Horizontal** gene transfer moves genetic material from one organism to another that is **not its offspring** — most common among prokaryotes.

::: {.callout-warning}
Horizontal transfer is why a single-gene tree is a **gene tree**, not necessarily a species tree.
:::
:::
:::

# Mitochondrial DNA

## Why mtDNA took over from allozymes

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
- Nuclear DNA is problematic in RFLP analysis; the method found much wider ecological application with **mtDNA**.
- Restriction mapping of mtDNA was an important improvement over allozyme electrophoresis.
- **No recombination during meiosis** — so networks of relationships among mtDNA lineages within and among populations can be constructed.
- mtDNA is usually inherited **maternally**, so only the behaviour and movements of females are effectively tracked.
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
![](/assets/loeng4/p11_1.jpg)

![](/assets/loeng4/p11_2.jpg){height="150px"}
:::
:::

## mtDNA — size and organisation

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](/assets/loeng4/p12_2.jpg){height="400px"}
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
- Size and organisation vary — **11–28 kbp** in animals.
- Animal mtDNA: **13 protein-coding**, **22 tRNA**, and **2 rRNA** genes.
- The mutation rate is relatively high — **5.8 × 10⁻⁸** substitutions per site per year in mammals, about **10× higher** than synonymous substitutions in nuclear protein-coding DNA.
- A non-coding region contains the **displacement (D) loop**.

![](/assets/loeng4/p12_1.jpg){height="120px"}
:::
:::

## Universal primers

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
- **Kocher et al. (1989)** were the first to develop what came to be called **universal primers**, for three regions of mtDNA — so a species can be studied **without prior sequence knowledge**.
- **Cytochrome b** is part of the electron transport chain and the main subunit of the cytochrome *bc*₁ and *b*₆*f* complexes; it is commonly used for phylogenetic relationships.
- Kocher's cyt *b* primers are the underlying reason sequences of this gene exist for so many species today.
- Mutation in one or both primer regions means "universal" primers do not work on all species — they are really just **versatile** primers.
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
![](/assets/loeng4/p13_1.jpg)
:::
:::

## Phylogeography

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
![](/assets/loeng4/p14_1.jpg){height="420px"}
:::
::: {.column width="55%"}
Because mtDNA does not recombine to any significant extent, lineage **networks** can be built and analysed in a **geographic** context.

**Avise et al. (1987)** coined the term **phylogeography** — encompassing both intraspecific phylogeny and geography.

Phylogeographic studies increased dramatically in the early 1990s and added substantially to our understanding of how current species distributions came into being.

::: {style="font-size:0.75em; color:#666;"}
Phylogeography of *Genetta genetta* from Bayesian analysis of cytochrome *b* + the left domain of the control region
:::
:::
:::

## Wolf vs coyote — three marker types

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
![](/assets/loeng4/p15_1.jpg)
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
| | mtDNA | Microsat. | SNP |
|---|---|---|---|
| Loci | one | 10–20 | millions |
| Copies/cell | thousands | few | few |
| Inheritance | maternal | biparental | biparental |
| Recombination | no | yes | yes |
:::
:::

# Identification of species

## How many species are there on Earth?

::: {.incremental}
- **Catalogue of Life**, 2019 Annual Checklist: information on **1,837,565 living** and **63,418 extinct** species.
- **Mora et al. (2011)** predicted globally around **8.7 million eukaryotic species**, of which about **2.2 million are marine**.
- Vertebrates — particularly birds and mammals — are comparatively very well documented.
- Molecular markers keep revealing **cryptic species** not previously recognised because of similar morphology.
:::

## The species problem

::: {.incremental}
- What is a species? Surprisingly, a significant and much-debated question in biology — **the species problem**.
- Biologists are now reconciled that **no single definition applies** to all species under all circumstances; at least **twenty-two species concepts** are in use.
- **Frankham et al. (2012)** found that different concepts often yielded different numbers of species and disparate groupings — with financial, legal, biological, and conservation implications.
- **Urmas Kõljalg** — the *species hypothesis*: more fluid and practical than species assignment.
:::

## Morphological species concept (MSC)

::: {.incremental}
- Historically, species were recognised by sharing a similar morphology, with individuals conforming to a **'type'**.
- Also known as the **typological species concept (TSC)**.
- A 'common sense' approach, and a frequently used definition in any first assessment.
- **Problems**: large phenotypic variation within or between populations; marked differences between the sexes, between juveniles and adults, or between developmental stages.
- **Cryptic species will be very under-recorded.**
:::

## Biological species concept (BSC)

::: {.incremental}
- Places emphasis on **reproductive isolation** between populations, not on morphology (Mayr 1942, 1963).
- A species is *"groups of actually or potentially interbreeding natural populations in the wild"*.
- Species are recognised on the basis of a **shared gene pool**; individuals are consequently often — but not always — similar in morphology.
- Rejected by most **botanists**, because of the large number of plants that reproduce asexually (Mayden 1997).
- The same problem arises in **microbiology**.
:::

## Phylogenetic species concept (PSC)

::: {.incremental}
- Places emphasis on **monophyletic genetic lineages**.
- Increasingly applicable alongside the rise in available molecular data.
- A species is *the smallest aggregation of populations (sexual) or lineages (asexual) diagnosable by a unique combination of apomorphous (derived) traits in comparable individuals descended from a shared common ancestor*.
- The difficulty is the **definition of unique traits**: phylogenetic lineages can be divided into ever smaller clades on the basis of trivial — but nonetheless shared and unique — traits.
:::

## Operational taxonomic unit (OTU)

::: {.incremental}
- An **OTU** is a group of organisms treated as a distinct evolutionary unit for the purposes of the research underway, which for various reasons has not — or cannot — be given a Linnaean binomial name.
- Mainly applied to **single-celled microorganisms**, though the concept is sometimes used for larger organisms, e.g. recently discovered sibling species awaiting recognition — **candidate species**.
- OTUs can be defined on morphology, molecules, or both — usually the latter. Very commonly by **% similarity of the rRNA gene**.
- **mOTU** — molecular operational taxonomic unit — is also used, particularly for cryptic species.
:::

## The concepts side by side

| Concept | Criterion | Strength | Where it fails |
|---|---|---|---|
| Morphological (MSC) | shared 'type' | fast, no lab | cryptic species, dimorphism, larvae |
| Biological (BSC) | reproductive isolation | mechanistic | asexual taxa, plants, microbes, fossils |
| Phylogenetic (PSC) | monophyly, apomorphies | uses molecular data | where to stop splitting |
| OTU / mOTU | % sequence similarity | operational, scalable | threshold is a convention, not a boundary |

::: {.notes}
The practical point for this course: the concept you choose determines the number you report. Say which one you used.
:::

## DNA barcoding

::: {.incremental}
- **DNA barcoding** (*liikide vöötkodeerimine*) is the use of short gene sequences from a **standardised portion of the genome** to identify species.
- The concept has been around for well over a decade, but high-throughput technology has moved it into a new phase of application.
- In the ideal case, a barcode marker **works for all species**.
- Markers applied to specific taxonomic groups are proving invaluable — and very cost-effective — for species boundaries, community ecology, functional trait evolution, trophic interactions, and conservation.
- Barcoding identifies a species by **matching the sequence to a reference library**.
:::

## Universal primers, revisited

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
![](/assets/loeng4/p24_1.jpg)
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
A usable barcode needs **conserved flanking regions** to anchor the primers, and a **variable region** in between that carries the species signal.

That trade-off — conserved enough to amplify, variable enough to discriminate — is the whole design problem.
:::
:::

## The barcoding idea

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
- The initial idea was simple: select one or a few genes shared by most — if not all — organisms, showing **large interspecific** (*liikide vaheline*) but **small intraspecific** (*liigisisene*) variation.
- Such sequences are the equivalent of species-specific barcodes.
- **Future outlook**: portable sequencers allow species identification **in the field**, even by people with little or no taxonomic training — e.g. with Nanopore.
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
![](/assets/loeng4/p25_1.jpg)
:::
:::

## DNA barcoding: COI

::: {.incremental}
- Early work focused on the mitochondrial **cytochrome oxidase subunit 1** (*cox1*), referred to as **COI** in barcoding studies (**Hebert et al. 2003**).
- Desirable properties: present in **high copy number** per cell; a partial sequence of about **650 bp** shows high interspecific and low intraspecific variation across organisms from insects to birds.
- **Problems**: many anaerobic organisms are excluded; interspecific variation of mtDNA in **plants and fungi** is often too low to be useful.
- **Mitogenomics** — the use of complete mtDNA sequences for identification and evolutionary studies, thanks to NGS.
:::

## COI — proof of concept

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](/assets/loeng4/p27_1.jpg)

::: {style="font-size:0.75em; color:#666;"}
Inter- and intraspecific COI distances among mayflies (Barr et al. 2005): means of 18.1% vs 1.1%
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](/assets/loeng4/p27_2.jpg){height="150px"}
![](/assets/loeng4/p27_5.jpg){height="150px"}

Mayflies (*ühepäevikulised*, Ephemeroptera) are widely used in the biomonitoring of aquatic habitats. Identifying adults by morphology requires substantial training, and **larval identification can be highly problematic**.
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
That gap between 1.1% and 18.1% is the "barcode gap". Where it closes, barcoding stops working.
:::

## DNA barcoding: plants and fungi

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
**Chloroplast (cpDNA) loci:**

- the intergenic spacer region **trnH-psbA**;
- ribulose bisphosphate carboxylase — **rbcL**;
- maturase K — **matK**.

**Nuclear loci:**

- the ribosomal DNA **internal transcribed spacer (ITS)** — *sisemine transkribeeritav speisser* — also used for fungi.
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
![](/assets/loeng4/p28_1.jpg)
:::
:::

# DNA metabarcoding and eDNA

## DNA metabarcoding

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
- A molecular alternative to classical taxonomic approaches for **high-throughput biodiversity assessment**, becoming a standard in biodiversity research.
- **DNA metabarcoding** — the use of NGS for automated identification of **multiple species** from a single bulk sample containing entire organisms, or from an environmental sample containing degraded DNA.
- **eDNA analysis** — presence/absence or quantification of large, multicellular organisms (usually vertebrates) in an environmental sample (usually water) using **species-specific PCR primers**.
- Metabarcoding also extends into **ancient DNA**.
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
![](/assets/loeng4/p30_1.jpg){height="180px"}

![](/assets/loeng4/p30_2.jpg){height="230px"}
:::
:::

## Limits of metabarcoding

::: {.incremental}
- Limited by its **dependency on PCR** and by the considerable investment needed to build comprehensive **reference libraries**.
- PCR problems: errors introduced during amplification from environmental samples (degraded template); primers need **conserved regions**, and PCR is **biased**.
- **The trade-off**: genes easy to amplify in all species are highly conserved and **underestimate** the true number of species; genes that describe species number better are **harder to amplify**.
:::

## Environmental DNA and RNA

::: {.incremental}
- Total eDNA contains **cellular DNA** (living cells or organisms) and **extracellular DNA** (from natural cell death and destruction of cell structure). Organisms shed DNA through mucous, skin cells, faecal matter, and degrading carcasses.
- It can be collected from essentially **any** environmental sample: soil, freshwater, seawater, snow, air.
- It lets researchers monitor species presence at **larger spatial scales**, more efficiently — particularly useful for **rare or hard-to-see aquatic organisms**.
- RNA is likewise found in environmental samples and is termed **eRNA**.
:::

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="58%"}
![](/assets/loeng4/p38_1.jpg)
:::
::: {.column width="42%"}
**What criteria constitute a species detection?**

The lack of consensus results from **context dependency** — total species diversity, sequencing depth, marker specificity — and from the trade-off between **stringency and uncertainty** when interpreting metabarcoding results.

Which markers? What frequency across samples?
:::
:::

## Limits of detection and quantification

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
![](/assets/loeng4/p39_1.jpg)
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
- **LOD** — the lowest concentration of target that can be detected with a defined level of confidence; the standard is a **95% detection rate**.
- **LOQ** — reflects the assay's capacity to **precisely quantify** copy number.

::: {style="font-size:0.75em; color:#666;"}
Klymus et al. 2019
:::
:::
:::

```{r lod, fig.height=2.8}
conc <- 10^seq(-0.5, 3, length.out = 200)
det  <- 1 / (1 + exp(-1.8 * (log10(conc) - 0.7)))   # illustrative logistic model
lod  <- conc[which.min(abs(det - 0.95))]

ggplot(data.frame(conc, det), aes(conc, det)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1, colour = "#990000") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.95, linetype = 2, colour = "grey40") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = lod,  linetype = 3, colour = "grey40") +
  annotate("text", x = lod, y = 0.35, hjust = -0.1, size = 3.6,
           label = paste0("LOD(95%) ~ ", round(lod), " copies/reaction")) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "target concentration (copies per reaction, log)",
       y = "detection probability") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
```

# Ancient DNA

## Ancient DNA

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
- **aDNA** — DNA isolated from ancient specimens, sediments, and similar material.
- It started with museum specimens of extinct species.
- **Pre-PCR**: Higuchi et al. (1984) studied mtDNA of the extinct **quagga**, whose last captive individual had died the year before — the work that inspired Michael Crichton's 1990 novel *Jurassic Park*.
- Studies moved from single individuals and populations to **understanding ancient ecosystems**.
- **Complete genomes of extinct species**: Miller et al. (2008) used 454 pyrosequencing to obtain **4.17 Gbp** from two woolly mammoth specimens.
:::

![](/assets/loeng4/p41_2.jpg){height="230px"}

## Technically challenging

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](/assets/loeng4/p43_1.jpg){height="200px"}

![](/assets/loeng4/p43_2.jpg){height="130px"}
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
- **Everything degrades over time** — fragmentation, chemical modification, and mutation accumulate.
- **Present-day contamination can lead to false conclusions**: the contaminant amplifies better than the target, every time.

![](/assets/loeng4/p43_3.jpg)
:::
:::

## The damage signature is the authentication

```{r adna-damage, fig.height=3.4}
pos <- 1:25
ct  <- 0.02 + 0.28 * exp(-0.35 * (pos - 1))     # illustrative C-to-T decay
oth <- rep(0.02, length(pos))

tibble::tibble(pos, `C-to-T substitutions` = ct, `other substitutions` = oth) |>
  pivot_longer(-pos) |>
  ggplot(aes(pos, value, colour = name)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#2E7D32", "#1565C0")) +
  labs(x = "position from the 5' end of the read", y = "substitution frequency",
       colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
```

Cytosine deamination at the fragment ends produces the **C→T excess in the first few positions**. Modern contaminant reads do not show it — which is why the damage pattern is used as *evidence of authenticity*, not just as a nuisance.

## 16S ribosomal RNA

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
![](/assets/loeng4/p46_1.jpg)

![](/assets/loeng4/p46_3.jpg){height="180px"}
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
![](/assets/loeng4/p46_2.jpg){height="300px"}

The **16S rRNA** gene is about **1600 bp** long and includes **nine hypervariable regions** (V1–V9) of varying conservation.

**V3 and V4** are the most commonly used — a suitable length for second-generation sequencing, combined with good variability.
:::
:::

## 18S ribosomal RNA

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
![](/assets/loeng4/p47_1.jpg)
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
- The **V4** region has the highest length polymorphism and is the **longest** variable region in the rRNA gene — **350 to 450 nt**.
- The **V9** region is characterised by high nucleotide variability in the centre, covering approximately **60 nt**.
:::
:::

## Standardised multi-omics of Earth's microbiomes

![](/assets/loeng4/p48_3.jpg)

**Earth Microbiome Project Ontology (EMPO)** categories: free-living vs host-associated, saline vs non-saline, and the substrate — a controlled vocabulary that makes thousands of independent studies comparable.

## Check yourself

<details>
<summary>Why is mtDNA so widely used in phylogeography?</summary>

High copy number (so it amplifies from poor material), no recombination (so lineages form a network), and maternal inheritance (so the genealogy is simple). The cost is that it tracks one locus and only the female line.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Why is COI a poor barcode for plants and fungi?</summary>

Their mitochondrial substitution rates are low, so interspecific COI variation is often too small to separate species. Plants use rbcL, matK, and trnH-psbA; fungi use ITS.

</details>

<details>
<summary>What is the "barcode gap", and what happens when it closes?</summary>

The gap between intraspecific and interspecific genetic distances — 1.1% vs 18.1% in the mayfly example. Where recent divergence, hybridisation, or introgression closes it, sequences cannot be assigned to species with any threshold.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Why does a detection near the LOD need more replicates, not more confidence?</summary>

Below the LOD, detection is stochastic: the target may not enter the reaction at all. Replication converts a single uncertain result into a detection frequency, which is the quantity you can actually interpret.

</details>

<details>
<summary>How is ancient DNA authenticated?</summary>

By its damage: short fragments and an excess of C→T substitutions at the fragment ends from cytosine deamination. Contaminating modern DNA is long and undamaged.

</details>
